planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in humus-rich, well-drained soil after the last frost once the ground has warmed.

directions: Set out dormant tubers or nursery divisions in spring after soil has warmed, spacing them a foot or more apart in soil enriched with compost. Plants die back completely with the first hard frost and resprout reliably from the fleshy tubers the following spring, so mark the location and mulch lightly over winter. This white-flowered form of the hardy begonia produces the same asymmetric wing-shaped leaves with red undersides as the species, but its pure white flower clusters glow in shade from late summer into fall. It self-seeds gently via small bulbils along the stems, making it an easy, reliable choice for brightening a dim woodland border without the tender begonia's need for winter storage.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Move divisions or started plants outdoors after all danger of frost has passed into rich, moisture-retentive soil in dappled shade.

directions: Grow this East African species from divisions of its swollen rhizomes or from young transplants set into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in a sheltered, part-shade spot. In frost-free or near-frost-free climates it forms a tall, cane-like clump that can be left in the ground year-round, while gardeners in colder regions dig and store the rhizomes indoors over winter like a dahlia. The large, orchid-like white-and-pink flowers are sweetly fragrant in the evening, a trait uncommon among impatiens, and the bold red-veined leaves give it a lush, tropical look at the back of a shaded border. It makes an unusually tall, scented centerpiece for a shade garden where most impatiens stay low and unscented.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in rich, well-drained soil in deep shade during spring or early fall.

directions: Plant this selection in loose, humus-rich soil beneath trees where little else will grow, and water regularly the first season while the thick rootstock establishes. Growth is slow, so choose a permanent spot; established clumps need only an annual topdressing of compost and are otherwise nearly maintenance-free. Compared to the straight species, this cultivar produces much larger, broader, heavily arching evergreen leaves in a bold architectural rosette, with the same inconspicuous fall flowers hidden at the base and red berries that follow. Its oversized leathery foliage makes a striking specimen or focal point in a deep-shade woodland bed where dramatic texture is otherwise hard to come by.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Asahi Cast Iron Plant (Morning Sun Aspidistra)

planting.note: Divide and transplant clumps into well-drained, humus-rich soil in deep shade during mild spring or fall weather.

directions: Set divisions into loose, well-drained soil in a spot that receives little to no direct sun, and keep the soil lightly moist until new growth appears. Once established this cast iron plant tolerates drought, deep shade, and general neglect better than almost any other shade perennial. Its glossy, dark green strap-shaped leaves emerge solid green but slowly develop creamy white tips and streaks toward the leaf ends as they mature, giving a two-toned effect distinct from the fully variegated cast iron cultivars. It works well as a tough, textural groundcover or container plant for the darkest corners of a porch or courtyard garden.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in consistently moist, rich soil in part to full shade after the last frost.

directions: Grow this cultivar in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded bed or large container, watering deeply whenever the soil surface starts to dry since the broad leaves wilt quickly in dry conditions. It rewards a sheltered spot near a downspout or pond edge where humidity stays high through summer. The rounded, glossy leaves have a pronounced undulating, wavy margin that catches light differently than the flatter-leaved forms of the species, and clusters of small daisy-like yellow flowers appear on tall stalks in fall. Its bold, rippled foliage adds strong textural contrast among ferns and hostas in a shaded border.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide clumps and replant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade during spring or fall.

directions: Plant divisions in loose, well-drained soil and water regularly the first year until the clumping rhizomes spread and fill in. Once settled it needs little care beyond an occasional trim of old or winter-damaged foliage. The arching, grass-like leaves are broader than common mondo grass and are edged in creamy white, brightening dim corners even before the arching spikes of small white summer flowers appear, which are followed by blue-violet berries. It makes a durable, low-maintenance edging or mass planting for shaded walkways where its variegated foliage provides year-round contrast against darker-leaved neighbors.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set rooted divisions or nursery plugs into moist, acidic, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade in spring or early fall.

directions: Space plugs or divisions evenly in loose, acidic soil amended with leaf mold, and water regularly until the creeping stems knit together into a solid mat, which is slower to fill in than the plain green form. Once established, shear back any all-green reverted shoots promptly to keep the planting uniformly variegated. Leaves are edged and mottled in creamy white around a soft green center, giving a brighter, more finely textured look than standard pachysandra, with the same small white spring flower spikes. It is a dependable, low, spreading evergreen for dry shade under trees where turf and most flowering perennials struggle.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or potted starts into well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring, spacing to allow the trailing stems to fill in.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in average, well-drained soil and keep evenly watered the first season as the trailing stems root along their length and knit into a dense mat. Trim back hard in early spring if growth becomes leggy or if any solid-green shoots revert, since the gold coloring is less vigorous than the plain species. The rounded leaves are centered in bright gold with a narrow dark green margin, brightening shaded ground far more than typical periwinkle, and single lavender-blue flowers appear in spring. It is useful as a slow, low, colorful groundcover for erosion control or filling gaps under shrubs where little sun reaches the soil.

common_name: Striped Lily of the Valley (Variegated Convallaria)

planting.note: Plant dormant pips or divisions in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade in fall, or in early spring where fall planting is impractical.

directions: Plant pips a few inches deep with the growing tip just below the soil surface in rich, cool, evenly moist soil, then leave undisturbed for several years as the rhizomes spread into a naturalized patch. Stripes are strongest on emerging spring foliage and tend to fade somewhat by midsummer, especially in warmer climates, so this form is best appreciated as an early-season accent. Each cream-and-green striped leaf pair frames the same intensely fragrant, nodding white bell flowers of the species in mid-spring. It brings extra visual interest to a shaded spring border even before the flowers open, and like the species it spreads readily to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover under trees.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
